title: Progressive fidelity fallbacks — notebook
content:
Quick brain-dump: progressive-fidelity fallbacks (rough PRD / experiment list).

Context / problem statement:
- We want hosted API customers to survive transient capacity or cost controls without a hard failure.
- Current behaviours: either full-quality model (slow/expensive) or an outright 429/over-capacity error; middle ground is inconsistent across routes.
- Need predictable, debuggable degradation paths that preserve critical semantics (safety, security) and surface clear SLO trade-offs to customers.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Default fallback profile that reduces token-cost by ~3x while maintaining >80% task success on common intents (summarization, Q&A, short replies).
- Failure mode telemetry surfaced in Console per-route: fallback count, latency delta, quality regression score.
- Customers can opt into progressive fallbacks per-route and pin a fallback policy.

Persona & user stories (short):
- As a product engineer, I want my chat route to degrade to shorter replies when capacity is throttled, rather than failing, so my app stays responsive.
- As an SRE, I want a transparent metric that shows how often fallbacks fire so we can tune autoscaling and avoid noisy degradation.
- As an enterprise admin, I want the private deployment to honor the same fallback contract but allow stricter safety checks.

Fallback taxonomy (brainstorm):
1) Fidelity reduction: shorter max_tokens, aggressive stop heuristics, compressed context (semantic compression).
2) Model downgrade: switch to a smaller-but-compatible model family (same tokenizer / schema).
3) Output shaping: prefer structured, terse answers (e.g., bullets) over verbose narratives.
4) Partial results: stream a stub/placeholder and queue full-quality generation asynchronously (for non-interactive use cases).
5) Degraded features: disable expensive functions (tool calls, web retrieval) and fall back to cached/local knowledge.

Initial experiment proposals:
- A/B: baseline vs progressive-fidelity profile A (50% token cap, verbatim compression) on a few high-volume product routes for 2 weeks. Primary metric: user-facing error rate down,  p50 latency maintained. Secondary: human eval quality on sampled prompts.
- Model downgrade matrix: measure quality delta and cost savings across {redwood-7b, 4b-quant, 2b-int8} for short chat vs long summarization workloads.
- Console UX: expose a per-route toggle + 3 predefined policy presets (conservative/standard/aggressive) with hover tooltips showing expected cost and p90 latency.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Implement fallback trigger logic: (a) capacity-signal from scheduler OR (b) latency SLO breach OR (c) explicit per-request header.
- Three fallback modes implemented: "shorten", "model-downgrade", "no-tools".
- Telemetry emitted: fallback_triggered, fallback_mode, latency_before, latency_after, tokens_saved (all as tags).
- Docs: short Console explainer + quickstart for customers.

Technical considerations / gotchas:
- Model equivalence: downgrades must preserve output schema (especially for function-calling/structured output). Need compatibility matrix per model.
- Safety: lower-capacity models may hallucinate more. Add stricter output filters when in fallback modes for sensitive routes.
- Billing & quotas: how to bill when fallback fires? show both attempted and executed tokens in usage so customers can reason about cost. Also consider stamping fallback events in billing logs.
- Cache interactions: prefix/KV caches must be aware of fallback mode to avoid serving stale or incompatible cached outputs.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (incubation): local dev spike, small-scope model downgrade proof-of-concept.
- Phase 1 (internal dogfood): enable on a few Redwood internal pipelines and one partner integration; collect quality deltas and telemetry.
- Phase 2 (beta customers): opt-in toggle in Console + API header; monitor retention/error rates.
- Phase 3 (general availability): enabled as opt-out per-route with recommended policies.

Metrics to track:
- fallback_rate_by_route (daily), ratio of requests that experienced any fallback.
- user_error_rate_by_route (compare pre/post).
- human_eval_quality_score (sampled weekly).
- cost_saved_tokens, estimated $ saved.
- customer_opt_out_rate (for GA).

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Should fallback policies be stateful per-session (stick to a downgrade for N requests) or evaluated per-request?
- UI: how to represent quality impact in Console without scaring customers? numeric delta vs qualitative labels?
- Billing: additive vs replaced token accounting for attempted vs executed tokens. Need finance input.
- Private deployments: should we enable automatic fallbacks by default or require operator opt-in for safety/compliance?

Notes for next meeting:
- Pull sample workloads from hosted-api top-20 routes and compute token length distribution.
- Get safety team quick read on hallucination risk for candidate small-models.
- Schedule GH spike: server#4821 (linked) is a starting stub for runtime hook points.

Rough timeline (very optimistic):
- Spike & experiments: 3–4 weeks.
- Internal dogfood: 2–3 weeks.
- Beta: 4–6 weeks.

Random thoughts / ideas to keep:
- Offer a "graceful-fallback" SLA upgrade for enterprise customers: guaranteed max-degradation and human-review path.
- Combine with routing policies: degrade to cheaper region or cheaper model depending on cost vs latency target.
- Consider a preview API that returns both 'high_fidelity' and 'fast_fidelity' candidate answers (consumer picks).

---
This doc intentionally messy — will extract a tidy PRD once spike data exists.
